summary: Defines two DNS resource record types, EUI48 and EUI64, for storing Ethernet-style hardware addresses in the DNS. It warns of serious privacy implications and says such addresses should not be published in the public DNS, intending the records for private namespaces.

eli5.summary: It adds DNS slots for the serial number on a network card, but warns not to put them where everyone can read.

questions: should mac addresses be published in dns
why is publishing mac addresses private
subtitle: DNS slots for storing hardware device addresses, with serious privacy warnings.

tldr.problem: Cable and other networks need to store hardware addresses (like MAC addresses) in the DNS, but there was no standard way to do it efficiently and interoperably.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7043 defines two new DNS resource record types: EUI48 (for 48-bit Ethernet addresses) and EUI64 (for 64-bit identifiers), with a standard hexadecimal format for both.
tldr.outcome: The records enable networks like DOCSIS to map IP addresses to hardware identifiers, but the RFC strongly warns that publishing such addresses creates severe privacy and security risks.

today: RFC 7043 remains an Informational RFC. It is not proposed for standardization and serves as a specification for private DNS deployments, particularly in cable networks. The primary implementation is in DOCSIS networks where it enables mapping of subscriber devices to IP addresses in restricted DNS zones.

sections.title: DNS Records for Hardware Addresses
sections.content:
The Domain Name System (DNS) holds many kinds of information, from IP addresses to mail servers. RFC 7043 adds two new record types: EUI48 and EUI64, for storing hardware addresses in the DNS.

EUI-48 and EUI-64 are 48-bit and 64-bit address formats defined by the IEEE for layer-2 networks. The most familiar example is the MAC address on Ethernet network cards, which is 48 bits. The RFC enables these addresses to be stored directly in DNS records rather than encoded awkwardly into other fields.
sections.eli5: The RFC adds a new type of DNS record that holds a hardware device's serial number, like the address stamped on your network card.

sections.title: Record Format and Examples
sections.content:
An EUI48 record stores a single 6-octet address, presented as six two-digit hexadecimal numbers separated by hyphens. The wire format (as sent on the network) is the 6 bytes in big-endian order. An example: host.example. 86400 IN EUI48 00-00-5e-00-53-2a

An EUI64 record is similar but stores 8 octets, presented as eight hex pairs with hyphens. The wire format is the raw 8 bytes. Example: host.example. 86400 IN EUI64 00-00-5e-ef-10-00-00-2a

Both record types are class independent (work with any DNS class) and have no special Time-to-Live requirements. IANA assigned type value 108 for EUI48 and 109 for EUI64.
sections.eli5: EUI48 is six pairs of hex digits (like 00-00-5e-00-53-2a) and EUI64 is eight pairs. They go into the DNS just like any other record.

sections.title: Why It Was Needed: DOCSIS Networks
sections.content:
The primary use case is in DOCSIS (cable modem) networks. When a cable company provides last-mile connectivity on behalf of a reseller, the cable company's DHCP server assigns IP addresses from the reseller's pool. The reseller knows the EUI-48 address of each subscriber's modem but not the IP address assigned to it. To map IP address back to subscriber identity, Canadian cable operators were required by regulators to publish EUI-48 to IP mappings in the DNS.

Before this standard, cable companies used ad-hoc encodings: addresses were stuck into domain names or stuffed into TXT records. RFC 7043 provides a clean, interoperable way to represent these mappings. The zones are published only in private DNS servers, restricted to authorized resellers, not the public Internet.
sections.eli5: Cable companies need to know which modem is which so they can match devices to customers. Instead of inventing their own ways to write that down in DNS, they can now use these standard record types.

sections.title: Privacy and Security Concerns
sections.content:
The RFC devotes a whole section to a serious warning: EUI-48 and EUI-64 addresses SHOULD NOT be published in the public DNS. The privacy implications are severe.

EUI-48 addresses are normally far more stable than IP addresses or DNS names. A device's MAC address typically does not change, even if the device moves to a different network or gets a new IP address. If an EUI-48 address is linked to an IP address in public DNS, a third party could track that device's location and behavior everywhere it connects, compromising user privacy.

Additionally, publishing these addresses could facilitate MAC cloning attacks: attackers could use a published MAC address to spoof a legitimate device and disrupt service or intercept data.

The RFC recommends mitigating these risks by restricting access to DNS zones containing these records to authorized clients only and provisioning them in private namespaces where access can be controlled.
sections.eli5: Hardware addresses are like a device's fingerprint—it stays the same everywhere. If someone puts your device's fingerprint in a public list, they can follow you from place to place. So this RFC says: keep these records secret, only in private networks where you trust everyone.

sections.title: Implementation Considerations
sections.content:
The specification has no effect on existing address resolution processes or protocols. Resolvers do not treat EUI48/EUI64 records specially. Systems that propose to use these records to modify or augment address resolution should specify how they handle address conflicts or multiple EUI48/EUI64 records for the same name.

The record types fit into the standard DNS architecture and existing DNS software can be extended to support them using the standard resource record framework.
sections.eli5: These records are just like any other DNS record—nothing special needed to store them or look them up.
